newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - WTO encouraged by request to delay Cuba panel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - WTO encouraged by request to delay Cuba panel.

text.p: The WTO world trade body on Wednesday said it was encouraged by an EU request to delay naming a panel to rule on complaints that U.S. legislation aimed against Cuba contravenes trade rules and voiced hopes of a rapid settlement.

World Trade Organisation (WTO) chief spokesman Keith Rockwell said the move was likely to be followed by consultations between the EU and United States to seek a compromise and settlement outside the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB).

European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said in a statement on Wednesday he had asked WTO chief Renato Ruggiero to delay naming the panel until February 20 in an attempt to reach a settlement with the U.S. over Washington's Helms-Burton Act
"The European Union is as eager as the United States to resolve the dispute over the Helms-Burton Act," Brittan said. "The EU does not want litigation for its own sake."

Rockwell said: "It has always been our view that parties which can resolve this bilaterally is a welcome development. If this is an indication that the U.S. and EU are heading in this direction, we would be very pleased."
Rockwell said the extension had not been considered as an option before and could bring more flexibility.

"The introduction of this new element gives some hope. The matter is now in the hands of the two players for at least another eight days," he said. "Consultations out of court tend to result in a more rapid resolution."
The EU and U.S. have been at odds for nearly a year over the act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy by the United States.

Among other things, the act allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts any foreign individuals or companies that benefit from investments in property confiscated by Havana since the communist revolution of 1959.
This part was suspended by U.S. president Bill Clinton in January, but the EU nevertheless proceeded with a complaint at the WTO.
The EU and U.S. have been unable to agree the composition of the panel and last week Brittan called for Ruggiero to intervene.

Washington has argued the issue should not go to the WTO as it involves U.S. national security issues and has threatened to ignore any WTO ruling on the matter -- a move analysts say could seriously undermine the two-year-old WTO which is based Geneva.
In his statement Brittan said Washington's claim was "not credible". Nevertheless, he said, he would ask Ruggiero to delay naming the panel to give time for further discussions with Washington.
